Only the supplied page subset was consulted; its headwords are lexical evidence, not a replacement transcription. Source: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . Corrections and English review notes are by the external AI reviewer identified in result.json.

runs.text: ſeparação como dos caſados entreſi, ou de ou

lines.note: Continues Ribet from f417: separation, as between spouses or other people. The initial is long ſ, not the OCR's roman F; ou continues as outras below without a supplied line-end hyphen.
Completes outras pessoas and ends the separation definition carried over from the preceding page.
This Ribiǒ entry concerns gains from interest-taking. The small accented preposition is à, not the OCR's d.
A separate Ribiǒ entry is explained by shibori hara, painful straining of the bowels. The repeated headword is not a duplicate to be removed.
Ribun first refers to interest gain, then ri no bun is introduced for the broader profit sense explained below.

runs.text: Ganho, ou proueito qualquer de mercancia, &c.

lines.note: Defines ri no bun as any gain or benefit from trade. The broader mercantile sense contrasts with the preceding specific interest sense.
Nashi no shita means beneath a pear tree. The headword Rica is retained without inserting an unestablished stop; the following example develops a caution about appearances.
The Japanese says not to adjust one's cap beneath a pear tree. Concer- begins the Portuguese verb concertar, to set right or adjust.

runs.text: tar o barrete de baixo da pereira, ſe acertar de

lines.note: Completes the instruction not to adjust the cap beneath the tree, then introduces the circumstance that the cap may be about to fall.

runs.text: ir pera cair da cabeça, pera que não cuidem

lines.note: Continues the cap's impending fall and gives the reason for restraint: avoiding suspicion. The opening reads ir rather than the OCR's tr; pera is preserved.

runs.text: que toma peras com amão. Vſa ſe em couſas q̃

lines.note: Onlookers might think the raised hand was taking pears. The explanation then generalizes the saying to situations requiring caution; q̃ remains unexpanded.

runs.text: he neceßario ter vigia, & precato pera que

lines.note: Advises watchfulness and precaution. The clause continues with the undesirable interpretation one is trying to prevent.
Finishes the warning against giving people grounds to think ill of someone. Cuidem, not euidem, is the visible verb in this context.
Ritoku wo kangayuru explains thinking about one's gain. The Portuguese starts the equivalent activity of considering or reflecting.
Adds continual pondering over one's own advantage. Proueito has t, not the OCR's n; parafuſar is retained as the historical expression.
Completes profit and begins an example making such calculation one's chief concern. Cui- continues the Portuguese translation on the next row.

runs.text: dar, & entender ſempre em ſeu proueito.

lines.note: Completes cuidar and explains continual attention to one's own benefit. This finishes the Rican example.
Richigui is explained by civility, refinement, and straightforwardness. Policia is the historical word in this moral and social gloss, not the OCR's Poicia.
The adjectival form describes a courteous, refined person. Sim- begins simples, whose sense is clarified by recto below.
Completes the description as straightforward and upright. Richiguina hito supplies the Japanese example of such a person.
This headword names a compound medicine. The faint i after R is present, and the vowel over u carries a caron; vari- starts varios.
Completes varios materiaes, indicating multiple ingredients. The gloss does not identify those ingredients individually.
Rikō here denotes sharpness or cleverness in speaking. A word boundary is visible between ſagacidade and no.
Rikō wo yū is speaking clever remarks. The scan supplies the paragraph sign omitted by OCR and a circumflex in the repeated form Ricôuo.
Qualifies those remarks as somewhat arrogant or proud. A further, less proper sense is introduced by the Latin Minùs, continued below.

runs.text: propriè, ſetoma por viueza, & feruor. Vt,

lines.note: Completes Minùs propriè and gives liveliness or vigour as the extended sense. The visible word is propriè, not proprdè; the tight ſetoma is preserved.
Rikō na mono exemplifies a lively, alert person. It illustrates the extended sense rather than the preceding boastful-speech sense.
Rikon is another entry for acuity and sagacity. The initial is R, not the OCR's F, and the next row supplies its example.
The Japanese describes a person of great discernment. Agu- starts the Portuguese superlative used to characterize him.
Completes agudissimo and calls the person very sagacious and discerning. Diſcreto has no extra o after c, correcting diſcoreto.
Defines someone who speaks acutely and sagaciously. The scan supports initial R and long ſ in ſagazmente, not the two f readings in the draft.
Adds the lively and alert sense to Ricôna, paralleling the earlier Ricô explanation.
Gives the adverb corresponding to Ricôna, with the same speaking or alertness senses. The grammatical label remains italic.

runs.text: Moſtra com algũa demaſia de agu

lines.note: Rikondate is an excessive display of cleverness. The printed agu continues as agudeza below, but no terminal hyphen is securely visible.
Completes agudeza and adds sagacity, specifying the qualities being ostentatiously displayed.
Names a discerning, sagacious person. The short agent entry is distinct from the adjectival form below.
The adjective describes a person as discerning, acute, and sagacious. The three Portuguese qualities are all retained.
Gives the adverbial member of the same rikon series. Its physical indentation is preserved despite its being a separate derivative.
Gives the nominal derivative expressing the degree or quality of cleverness, without a separate Portuguese gloss. The stop after it is visible.
Hana wo tatsuru explains arranging flowers upright. Va- begins the Portuguese vessel in which they are placed.
Completes vaso and compares the arrangement to a bouquet. Rikka wo suru supplies the Japanese example of making the arrangement.

runs.text: Seis eſpecies de mezinhas as quaes

lines.note: Introduces six kinds of medicinal substances. The relative clause below records the dictionary's claim about their keeping properties.

runs.text: nunca ſe danão por mais velhas que ſejão.

lines.note: The historical gloss says these substances do not spoil however old they become. This is the source's statement, not a modern medicinal recommendation.
Kachimichi explains rikugi as a land route. The following example illustrates difficulty travelling over that route.
Begins a sentence in which snow has accumulated on the land route. Uma no at the right edge governs the horses' feet on the next row.
Completes the Japanese clause: the horses could not keep their footing or lift their feet. The upright citation is Taif.; the book number is visibly 28, not the OCR's 2.

runs.text: Quanto he por terra tendo chouido muita neue,

lines.note: Begins the Portuguese translation, describing much snow having fallen on the land route. Chouido is retained as the source's historical wording; the translation continues in column 2.

runs.text: & atolando os pès dos caualos nella de manei-

lines.note: Continues the snowbound journey: the horses' feet sink into the snow. The grave in pès and the divided manei- are retained.

runs.text: ra que os não podião aleuantar, &c.

lines.note: Completes maneira and says that the horses could not lift their feet. This finishes the translation begun at the bottom of column 1.
Mutsu wo awasuru explains combining six parts. The Portuguese enumerative abbreviation ends with a stop, not the OCR's hyphen; the six directions are listed next.

runs.text: os quatro rumos principaes, & aparte do Ceo

lines.note: Gives the four principal directions plus the skyward part. The supposed l after Ceo is the right-hand rule, not a letter.

runs.text: ſobre a cabeça, & a inferior da terra.

lines.note: Completes the six-part scheme with above the head and below toward the earth. These are directional components, not new entries.
Mutsu no gei means six arts. Seis and liberaes are the clear Portuguese readings, correcting Ses and liheraes.

runs.text: que ha em Iapão, & na china. ſ.

lines.note: Introduces the named arts as practiced in Japan and China. Rei is the first item, and ga- continues gacu on the next line; the OCR's extra a after Rei was a comma.
Completes gacu and lists the remaining arts, then cross-refers to Gueinô. The Japanese names remain roman within this Portuguese enumeration and cross-reference.

runs.text: Andas, ou carro em que caualga o

lines.note: Defines a royal litter or carriage. Carro, not carto, is visible in the Portuguese; the passenger is identified below.
Completes the carriage definition with the king. Rey is Portuguese and italic, not the OCR's roman Japanese-looking Ru.

runs.text: Razão, ou palauras com que hum ar-

lines.note: Rikutsu is explained as reasons or words used in arguing. The gloss specifies the manner of that argument on the next row.
Completes arrezoa and characterizes the reasoning as lengthy or troublesome. Ricut begins the compound naming a person who argues that way.
Iy completes rikutsu-ii, a person who produces such arguments. The Portuguese directly refers back to the prolix or troublesome manner just described.
Rikutō names a book of military art. The caron differentiates this title from the preceding unmarked Ricut.
The gloss pairs mental sharpness with slowness of understanding. The contrast is intentional, not a contradictory word to be corrected.
Rihatsu is equated with Saican and defined as liveliness and sagacity. Another equivalent follows on the next row.
Adds discernment as an equivalent of Rifat. The tilde's printed carrier is retained rather than modernizing the ending.
Names an alert, sagacious person. The jin ending distinguishes the person noun from the quality itself.
Gives the adjectival form with the same alertness and sagacity sense. Idem refers to the description immediately above.
Gives the corresponding adverb. Its indentation and the italic grammatical label are preserved.
Gives the nominal derivative for the quality or degree of sagacity. No separate gloss is printed; the final stop is visible.
Rihi contrasts right and wrong, or reason and its absence. The example has the object particle uo in Rifiuo, not the OCR's no; the whole Japanese word is roman.
Wakuru completes the instruction to distinguish right from wrong. Dicernir is retained without adding the s of a more familiar spelling.
Adds justice and injustice as the paired objects of discrimination. It completes the Rifi example.
Kotowari wo tsukusazu is not fully examining or exhausting the reasons. The damaged vowel in naõ is a, not u; exa- continues the Portuguese verb below.
Completes the failure to examine the reasons properly and introduces an unreasonable command. The repeated headword contains f, not OCR t.
Translates the command as lacking reason and justice. The gloss is wholly Portuguese and remains italic.
The adjective describes an unreasonable thing. Rifujinna retains the f of the headword, correcting the OCR's long-s substitution.
Gives the adverb 'unreasonably'. Both R and f are supported by the adjacent forms, replacing the OCR's Birujinni.
Rigai is glossed as outside reason. The historical gua spelling is kept rather than replaced with a modern romanization.
Madara ushi identifies a mottled or piebald bovine. The Portuguese specifically says a spotted cow; the marked headword is retained.

runs.text: O apertar, ou conuencer com a força

lines.note: Rizeme is pressing or convincing someone through the force of reason. The phrase specifying that force and the example continue below.
Completes 'the force of reason' and gives hito wo rizeme ni suru, subjecting someone to that pressure. The OCR inserted an extra i at the boundary after Fitouo.
Rijun is equated with ritoku and glossed as gain or benefit. This is an independent profit entry after the reasoning vocabulary.
The first Rimot entry gives gain, advantage, or yield. Fruito retains its historical vowel sequence.
A second entry gives the Buddhist expression rimot no owari. Its translation begins 'end or completion'; Fim, not Pim, is the visible word.
Completes consumação and describes the fulfilment of human salvation in the source's terminology. The upright Bup. identifies the Buddhist usage.

runs.text: Hũa maneira de campainha, ou batega

lines.note: Rin denotes a kind of small bell or metal basin-like sounding vessel. Its physical construction is described on the next row.
The vessel is round and has no clapper. Rin wo utsu means striking it, and Latin l introduces another verb below; the initial is R, not B.

runs.text: Tanger eſta batega. Item, Em algũas

lines.note: Narasu is the alternative for sounding the vessel. The Portuguese then introduces a regional extension of the word's meaning.

runs.text: partes do Ximo ſe toma gèralmente por cam-

lines.note: In some parts of Ximo the term is used generally for a bell. The l missing in the OCR is visible, and the mark over e is read as a single grave stroke: gèralmente, not normalized geralmente. Grave versus a worn tilde is a nonblocking caveat. Ximo has the sloping lowercase forms of the surrounding italic text.
Completes campainha and ends the regional bell sense of Rin.

runs.text: ira, ou pedaço depano, ou peça q̃ ſe a-

lines.note: This separate Rin entry is a strip or piece of cloth added to a garment. The upright capital T and sloping ira lead to retention of the draft's mixed font boundary rather than whole-word normalization; the capital's exact font remains a nonblocking caveat. The abbreviated q̃ is preserved.

runs.text: crecenta no cabeção, & dianteira dos veſti-

lines.note: Completes acrecenta and locates the added strip at the neck and front of garments. Veſti- continues below.
Completes vestidos and records Yeri as the term used in Cami. Rin wo sasu is the separate Japanese example for adding the strip; Yeri and Cami occur inside the Portuguese regional explanation.

runs.text: Por, ou acrecẽtar no cabeção dos veſtidos de

lines.note: Translates the example as putting or adding a strip at the neck of Japanese garments. The tilde abbreviation in acrecẽtar remains unexpanded.

runs.text: Iapão algũa tira doutro pano, peça, &c.

lines.note: Specifies a strip or piece of another cloth. The scan has singular peça and the normal final &c., not the OCR's peças and mixed-font &oc.
